tagline: Chocolate, comics, and the capital of Europe
overview:
Belgium is a small, crowded country on the North Sea, about the size of Maryland, squeezed between France, the Netherlands, Germany, and Luxembourg. Nearly 12 million people live here, which makes it one of the most densely populated countries in Europe. It is really two main regions in one: Flanders in the north, where people speak Dutch, and Wallonia in the south, where they speak French. A small community in the east speaks German, so Belgium has three official languages. The capital, Brussels, is officially bilingual.

Brussels is also the home of the European Union's main institutions and the headquarters of NATO, which is why it is often called the capital of Europe. Belgium is a federal constitutional monarchy with a king and a parliament. Belgians are famous for chocolate, waffles, fries served with mayonnaise, hundreds of kinds of beer, and comic-strip heroes like Tintin and the Smurfs. The medieval cities of Bruges and Ghent, with their canals and stepped-gable houses, look much as they did 500 years ago.
landAndNature: Belgium slopes gently upward from the sea. Along its short 67-kilometer coast run wide sandy beaches and dunes, backed by flat polder farmland that was once drained from the sea. Central Belgium is a fertile plateau of farms and towns cut by the Scheldt and Meuse rivers. In the southeast rise the Ardennes, a rolling region of dense forests, rocky river gorges, and peat bogs; the highest point, the Signal de Botrange, is just 694 meters. Wild boar and red deer roam the Ardennes woods. The climate is mild and famously rainy. Each April the Hallerbos forest near Brussels turns into a carpet of purple-blue bluebells that draws visitors from around the world.
peopleAndCulture: Belgians take food seriously. Fries, which Belgians insist they invented, are sold in paper cones from street stands, moules-frites pairs them with mussels, and chocolate pralines were created in Brussels in 1912. Trappist monks brew some of the world's most respected beers, and Belgian beer culture is on UNESCO's heritage list. Comics are treated as an art form: Hergé created Tintin, Peyo drew the Smurfs, and Brussels is decorated with dozens of giant comic murals. At the Carnival of Binche, men in wax masks and ostrich-feather hats throw oranges to the crowd. The saxophone was invented by Belgian Adolphe Sax. Cycling legend Eddy Merckx and the national soccer team, the Red Devils, are sporting heroes, and painters Van Eyck, Rubens, and Magritte were all Belgian.
history: Julius Caesar wrote about the Belgae, Celtic tribes who lived here 2,000 years ago. In the Middle Ages, cloth-making towns like Bruges and Ghent were among the richest in Europe. The region then passed through Burgundian, Spanish, Austrian, French, and Dutch hands; Napoleon was finally defeated at Waterloo, just south of Brussels, in 1815. Belgium won independence from the Netherlands in 1830 and chose Leopold I as king. King Leopold II ran the Congo in Africa as his personal property from 1885 to 1908, a brutal period in which millions of Congolese died; Belgium then ruled it as a colony until 1960. Germany invaded neutral Belgium in both world wars, and the trenches of Flanders and the Battle of the Bulge in the Ardennes are remembered worldwide. Belgium helped found the European Union.
funFacts: Belgium's highway network is lit so brightly at night that astronauts can pick it out from space.
In 2010 and 2011 Belgium went 541 days without an elected government, a world record at the time.
The Atomium in Brussels, built for the 1958 World's Fair, is a 102-meter model of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.
The town of Spa gave the world the word spa; its mineral springs have drawn visitors since the 1300s.
Continental Europe's first passenger railway opened in Belgium in 1835, running between Brussels and Mechelen.
